title: Checkpoint: Instruments
objective: After this level you can compare how strings, woodwinds, brass, percussion and voices make sound.
summary: Each instrument shakes the air its own way, and each note carries harmonics. Which harmonics sound, and how strongly, is its timbre: why the same A never sounds alike.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 finale: a flute, a violin and a clarinet all play the same A.
cards.body: All three can play the A at 440 Hz. You'd still tell them apart with your eyes shut. This chapter showed what vibrates in each instrument; one last idea explains why the same note sounds different on every one of them.

cards.headline: Five ways to shake the air
cards.body: Strings: a plucked, bowed or struck string, made loud by a body. Woodwinds: air in a tube, set going by an edge or a reed. Brass: air in a tube, set going by buzzing lips. Percussion: a stretched skin, or the instrument's own body. Voice: two vocal folds, shaped by throat, nose and mouth. Different starters, one job: shake the air.

cards.headline: Why the same A sounds different
cards.body: An instrument never plays just one frequency. Along with the fundamental, the note you name, it sounds harmonics: Level 14's ladder of whole-number multiples. Which harmonics sound, and how strongly, sets its timbre, or tone color. Flutes and violins produce all the harmonics, while clarinets emphasize the odd ones. Same pitch, same loudness, different blend.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing from this chapter: same note, different blend of harmonics.

cards.fact: A tuning fork sounds so pure because it has almost no overtones.
cards.context: Take the harmonics away and a note sounds plain and clear, like a tuning fork. Every instrument in this chapter adds its own blend of harmonics on top of the note. That blend is its timbre, as personal as a voice on the phone.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 complete
learned: How every instrument makes sound by shaking the air, and how to sort them by what vibrates.
Why a shorter, tighter or lighter string, or a shorter tube, plays a higher note.
How brass players pick notes from a tube's hidden ladder with their lips and valves.
Why the same note sounds different on a flute, a violin and a clarinet.

questions.prompt: What does an instrument's timbre, or tone color, depend on?

options.label: Only how loudly it is played
options.rationale: Two instruments at the same loudness still differ.

options.label: Only the pitch of its fundamental
options.rationale: The same pitch can have different timbres.

options.label: How fast sound travels from it
options.rationale: Sound travels at the same speed from every instrument.

options.label: Which harmonics sound, and how strongly

questions.explanation: Timbre comes from which harmonics sound along with the fundamental, and how strong they are.

questions.prompt: A flute and a clarinet play the same pitch at the same loudness. Why do they still sound different?

options.label: The clarinet plays a slightly higher note
options.rationale: They are on the same pitch.

options.label: Their harmonics differ: clarinets emphasize the odd ones
The flute has no harmonics at all
Sound from a flute travels faster
options.rationale: All sounds cross the air at the same speed.

questions.explanation: Flutes produce all the harmonics while clarinets emphasize the odd ones, so their timbres differ.

questions.prompt: From Level 14's brass: what happens when a trumpet player presses a valve?

options.label: The air takes a detour through extra tubing
A hole opens in the side of the tube
options.rationale: That's how a woodwind's tone holes work.

options.label: The mouthpiece tightens the lips
options.rationale: Lip tension is the player's job.

options.label: A damper stops the tube vibrating

questions.explanation: A valve sends the air through extra tubing, making the tube longer and the notes lower.

questions.prompt: From Level 16's piano: what could Cristofori's hammer keyboard do that a harpsichord couldn't?

options.label: Play more than one note at a time
Play without any strings
Play soft or loud depending on touch
Stay in tune forever

questions.explanation: A harpsichord plucks at much the same volume; the piano's hammers strike harder when you press harder.

questions.prompt: From Level 13's woodwinds: what starts the air vibrating in an oboe or a bassoon?

options.label: Air blown against an edge
Buzzing lips on a cup mouthpiece
A single reed on a mouthpiece
A double reed

questions.explanation: Oboes and bassoons use a double reed; clarinets and saxophones a single reed; flutes an edge.
